\section[considerar]{considerar — to consider; to regard as}

\label{lesson:ES-C576-considerar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to seem, then the Spanish for to keep.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: considerar}
\textbf{considerar} — \textquotedblleft{}to consider; to regard as\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Considero que es una buena idea.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I consider it a good idea.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Considerar que} + indicative gives your opinion; \emph{considerar algo importante} is to regard it as important.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{considerar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{considerare} 'to examine closely, to scrutinize', built from \emph{con-} and, by the usual account, \emph{sidus} 'star', as if first to watch the stars (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{considerar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{considerar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{considerar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to seem, then the Spanish for to keep, then say \emph{considerar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does considerar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To consider; to regard as\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sostener]{sostener — to maintain, to claim; to hold up}

\label{lesson:ES-C576-sostener}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to keep, then the Spanish for to consider.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sostener}
\textbf{sostener} — \textquotedblleft{}to maintain, to claim; to hold up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sostengo que el plan es bueno.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I maintain that the plan is good.}
\end{quote}

Like \emph{tener}: \emph{sostengo, sostuve}. In a debate \emph{sostener que} is to argue that.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sostener} is inherited from Latin \emph{sustinere} 'to hold up, to support', built from \emph{sub(s)} and \emph{tenere} 'to hold' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sostener}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sostener}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{sostener}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to keep, then the Spanish for to consider, then say \emph{sostener} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la creencia]{la creencia — the belief}

\label{lesson:ES-C576-creencia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to consider, then the Spanish for to maintain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la creencia}
\textbf{la creencia} — \textquotedblleft{}the belief\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es una creencia muy antigua.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is a very old belief.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Las creencias} — beliefs, often religious ones.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{creencia} is built on \emph{creer} with the ending \emph{-encia}; \emph{creer} is inherited from Latin \emph{credere} 'to trust, to believe' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la convicción]{la convicción — the conviction, the firm belief}

\label{lesson:ES-C576-conviccion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to maintain, then the Spanish for the belief.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la convicción}
\textbf{la convicción} — \textquotedblleft{}the conviction, the firm belief\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Lo digo con convicción.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I say it with conviction.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tener la convicción de que} — to be firmly convinced that.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{convicción} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{convictio} 'proof', built on \emph{convincere} 'to overcome, to prove', from \emph{vincere} 'to win' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to maintain, then the Spanish for the belief, then say \emph{la convicción} again

\section[la postura]{la postura — the stance, the position; posture}

\label{lesson:ES-C576-postura}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the belief, then the Spanish for the conviction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la postura}
\textbf{la postura} — \textquotedblleft{}the stance, the position; posture\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¿Cuál es tu postura sobre el tema?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{What is your position on the issue?}
\end{quote}

In a debate, \emph{la postura} is the side you take; for the body it means posture.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{postura} comes from Latin \emph{positura} 'position, arrangement', built on \emph{ponere} 'to put, to place' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
